1:
Mark opens with a title rather than a genealogy, and the witnesses spend the verse deciding what kind of sentence it is. Robertson notes there is no article in the Greek and allows that the phrase may have served as a heading for the paragraph about the Baptist, or as a superscription for the whole Gospel, placed either by Mark or a scribe; he borrows from Swete the point that every writer chooses a different starting point, Mark the work of the Baptist where John begins with the Preincarnate Logos. Ellicott sees a transition caught in mid-air, the word standing between its earlier sense of the good news of the kingdom and its later sense of a book. Barnes rejects the reading that would make it mean history or life, since Mark says nothing of the early life of the Saviour. Pseudo-Jerome insists that the four Gospels are one and one Gospel in four, and lays out the three languages of the name: Jesus in Hebrew, Soter in Greek, Salvator in Latin, and Christus, Messias, Unctus, that is King and Priest.

Why the narrative starts where it does is answered the same way by voices that agree on little else. Gill guards against the obvious misreading, that the gospel first began to be preached here, when it was preached by Isaiah and to Abraham and as early as Eden; the sense is only that this narrative begins with the ministry of John, the law and the prophets having been until him. Wesley says the evangelist speaks with strict propriety, the beginning of the Gospel being the account of John and the Gospel itself the rest of the book. Calvin makes it a divine intention rather than an editorial one: the Heavenly Father chose that the life of his Son should be buried in silence until the time of full revelation, which is why the evangelists pass from his earliest infancy to his thirtieth year. Lightfoot makes the Baptist the gate and entrance of the whole dispensation, opening a new church by a new sacrament of admission and bringing in, for justification by works, a doctrine of faith and repentance.

The last three words draw the only textual note and the sharpest theology. Robertson reports that some manuscripts omit Son of God while the great mass have it, and judges that if Mark wrote the words there is no reason to doubt them, since he uses the phrase elsewhere. Barnes reads the title as placed there to attract attention and secure respect, since this is no common history of a hero or philosopher. Bede compares the two openings and finds a deliberate ascent: Matthew names the Son of David and of Abraham, Mark the Son of God, that from less things our sense may by degrees mount up to greater. Hilary insists on the difference the word carries, that we are sons by adoption while he is Son by origin, in truth and not in name, by birth and not by creation.

Two questions of authorship are raised and left open. On composition, Clarke reports that the primitive fathers, Papias and Irenaeus and Tertullian and Eusebius among them, held Mark to be only the amanuensis of Peter; that Augustine appears to have been the first to maintain that Mark abridged Matthew; and that others suppose a compilation out of Matthew and Luke — most of which, he says, are conjectures with little foundation. Barnes states the tradition as uniform, that Mark was the interpreter of Peter and wrote under his eye. On readership, Clarke argues from the Latin words in the book that it was written for the Roman people, and explains on that ground why the genealogy is wholly passed by. Jerome has Mark a Levite who had served the priesthood, converted and writing in Italy, and takes the opening cry as showing the order of the election of Levi.
2:
The citation is the chapter's real crux, because it names Isaiah and then quotes Malachi first. Jerome states the difficulty flatly: this is not written in Isaiah but in Malachi, the last of the twelve prophets. The Greek catena concedes that it may be said to be a mistake of the writer, then offers the better account, that two prophecies delivered in different places by two prophets have been compressed into one and referred back to the elder, who was the first to intimate the sense. Bede gives two answers and is candid about the second. The sense of the words is found in Isaiah in many places, most clearly in the line about the voice in the wilderness; or else Isaiah occurred to Mark's mind instead of Malachi, as often happens, and he would without doubt have corrected it when reminded by readers while he was yet in the flesh, unless he thought that, his memory being then ruled by the Holy Spirit, the substitution had a purpose — for whatever the Spirit spoke by one prophet belonged to all.

The textual question runs alongside the exegetical one and divides the moderns cleanly. Clarke argues that the reading should be Isaiah, on the authority of the Codex Bezae and the Vatican and several versions, and supposes the plural was introduced so that the reference might comprehend both prophets. Ellicott agrees that the better manuscripts give Isaiah and reasons about scribal habit in the same direction, that a general reference is more likely to have been specialised by a transcriber than the reverse; he adds that this is the only prophetic quotation Mark makes on his own account, and connects the silence with his writing for Gentiles. Robertson sorts the witnesses by class and adds that Isaiah is named as chief of the prophets, chains of quotations being common. Gill and Lightfoot argue the other way from Jewish usage: two prophets are cited and Isaiah is the last of them, and naming only the later of two testimonies is, Lightfoot says, without all example.

On what the messenger is, the fathers converge and then part. Theophylact calls the Forerunner an angel on account of his angelic life, and reads before thy face as meaning that those walk next to kings who are their greatest friends; the way, he adds, is the New Testament and the paths the Old, because a path is already trodden. Bede allows the title only by the dignity of the office, since the Greek word means messenger in Latin, and takes the occasion to reject the view that John was an angel by community of nature; he then sets voice before Word as sound necessarily precedes speech. Calvin notices that the person of the quotation changes, the prophet having God say before me where Mark has God address the Son, and judges that Mark meant only to express the prophet's meaning more clearly.

What the crying is for divides into a moral reading and a historical one. Pseudo-Jerome hears a cry because we cry to the deaf and to those afar off and when we are indignant, all of which applied, and because the place was deserted by prophet, priest and king; he then turns the straightening of paths into a rule about neighbours, since he who loves himself and corrects no one turns aside to the right, as Eli did, and he who rebukes well but acts badly turns aside to the left, as the Scribes and Pharisees. Robertson keeps to the original setting, where God is coming to deliver his people from captivity in Babylon and the prophet cries to make ready, and notes that John used this very language of himself to the committee from the Sanhedrin. Cyril of Jerusalem puts the hinge where the chapter puts it, that baptism is the end of the Old Testament and the beginning of the New.
4:
Mark drops into the Forerunner's work without preliminaries, and Ellicott makes that abruptness the point: no other Gospel passes so completely in medias res, with no birth, no infancy and no pre-existence, since Mark is here as elsewhere emphatically the Evangelist of action. Robertson presses the verb, that John's coming was an epoch and not a mere event, and that he is described as the baptizing one. Gill corrects the picture the word wilderness invites, since it was not a wild uninhabited place but had many cities, towns and villages in it; he also notices that baptizing stands before preaching though John certainly came preaching first. Clarke takes the name itself as the theme, the original being compounded of the grace or mercy of Jehovah, which he calls a most proper name for the forerunner of the God of All Grace. Pseudo-Jerome reads it the same way and makes the narrative begin with grace, since John means the grace of God, and adds that what the bridegroom brings to perfection the friend of the bridegroom introduces.

Whether the baptism itself remitted sins is the first real division. Bede draws the line as sharply as it can be drawn: remission is given only by the baptism of Christ, so the text says preaching and not giving, and John preached a baptism which could remit sins precisely because he could not give it. Theophylact says the same in fewer words, that John's baptism had not remission but only brought men to penitence, and preached that to which penitence led. Robertson reaches a similar result by grammar rather than theology, calling the phrase difficult to translate and holding that with reference to is as good a rendering as is possible, since John did not mean that the baptism obtained forgiveness. Clarke renders it toward the remission and divides the work, repentance preparing the soul and baptism being the type or pledge of it. Ellicott alone leans the other way, taking it that then as evermore repentance was followed by forgiveness, even though the blood which availed for that forgiveness had not yet been shed.

On what the crowds were doing, the witnesses supply custom and observation in turn. Robertson hears in the tense a steady stream of people who kept coming, and calls the public confessions a thing that would produce a profound impression now; he adds that the symbol was already in use among the Jews for proselytes, so that John is treating the nation itself as pagans who need to come back. Clarke supplies the custom exactly: no proselyte was admitted to baptism until he had in the most solemn manner renounced all idolatrous worship and promised an unreserved submission to the law of Moses. Bede takes the confessing as a pattern held out to all who desire baptism, an example of owning sins and promising a new life. Ellicott notices a small editorial habit in the phrase about the river, which he reads as written for people unfamiliar with the topography of Palestine.

Two of the older voices leave the plain sense for figures. Pseudo-Jerome has John as the bridegroom's friend bringing the bride to Christ, as a servant brought Rebecca to Isaac, and reads her descent from the camel as the Church humbling herself on seeing her husband; he then interprets the name of the river as an alien descent, so that those who were aliens to God by pride are made lowly by baptism and thus exalted. Cyril of Jerusalem keeps the medical figure instead: they first showed their wounds and then he applied the remedies, and the call to put off the slough of a former life is addressed to a generation of vipers who must rub off the old skin at the strait and narrow gate. Wesley compresses the whole verse into a definition, preaching repentance and baptizing as a sign and means of it.
6:
The clothing gets more attention than any other detail in the paragraph, and the first question is what the material was. Robertson settles it plainly: not camel's skin but rough cloth woven of camel's hair, and he notes that dried locusts are considered palatable and that the wild or mountain honey was bountiful in the clefts of the rocks, some Bedouins still making their living by gathering it. Lightfoot goes to the Talmudists, where the phrase would be read camel's wool, and reports the rule forbidding a garment of camel's hair with even one thread of linen woven in as a mixture of different kinds; he also collects the opinion of R. Samuel Bar Nachman that the coats God made for Adam were of camel's hair, alongside the curious variant in the law of R. Meir which read garments of light for garments of skins. Gill supplies the social fact, that it was usual for penitents and men of austere life to live in deserts and wear coarse apparel, and instances a man known by his goat's hair garment because it cut his flesh and so might atone for him.

The fathers read the same clothing as a sermon. Bede takes hair rather than wool as the mark of an austere garb against effeminate luxury, and the girdle of skins, worn as Elias wore it, as a mark of mortification; he reads the diet as the man's inward walk, since in honey there is sweetness and in locusts swiftness of flight, and John's preaching had a sweetness for the multitude that soon ended when they understood he was not the Christ. Theophylact turns each detail into a judgement on the hearers: the hair signifies the grief of the penitent, the girdle of skins the dead state of the Jewish people, and the locusts their intellectual food, since the people leapt up and sank again as locusts do, and ate honey that came from the prophets but was wild and not domestic, for they had the Scriptures and did not rightly understand them. Gregory refers the food forward instead, to the Lord who took the sweetness of the barren Gentiles in the wild honey and the Jews in the locusts, who leapt upwards in words and fell down by their actions.
7:
On the announcement that follows, the voices agree about the motive and divide about the wording. The Gloss says the disclaimer was made to do away with the opinion of the crowd that John himself was the Christ. Bede notices how carefully the announcement is pitched, proclaiming the Lord not yet as God but only as a man mightier than himself, because the hearers were not capable of so great a Sacrament, and then declaring his divinity covertly, since none but God can give the grace of the Holy Ghost. Pseudo-Chrysostom refuses to harmonise the two reports: to loose the latchet and to carry the shoes are not the same act, and the Evangelists, following the order of the narrative and unable to err, mean that John said each in a different sense, however variously commentators have expounded them. Ellicott treats it as a deliberate choice of the more vivid phrase, since stooping to loosen the sandals was the act of the servant who afterwards carried them and expressed the menial character of the office better. Robertson reports that Gould called it a sceptical depreciation of himself, thinks it sincere, and notes that Mark alone gives the touch; Clarke adds that the shoe was properly only a sole tied about the foot with thongs.

Two figures are drawn from the shoe and one contrast from the water. Gregory offers both: shoes are made from the skins of dead animals, so the Lord coming incarnate appeared shod, having assumed the dead skins of our corruption; or else the ancient custom applies, by which the kinsman who offered himself as husband took off the shoe of the man who refused the woman, so that John disclaims the name of Bridegroom as above his deserts. Theophylact has John loosing the latchet of all others, that is the bands of their sin, and unable to loose Christ's because he found no sin in him. On the last verse Jerome puts the difference in one line, that water is the ministry of man while the Spirit is ministered by God. Ellicott notes that Mark omits the fire which Matthew joins to the Holy Ghost, possibly as less intelligible to Gentile readers, and Cyril of Jerusalem supplies the reason the others leave out, that the descent of the Holy Ghost was in fiery tongues.
9:
Mark brings Jesus in from Nazareth without warning, and the moderns note how much the compression costs and gains. Ellicott points out that Mark supplies the town where Matthew gives only the province, and that the language of the next clause is more boldly vivid than the other Gospels, the heavens being rent open rather than opened. Robertson makes the same point from the participle, which splits the sky like a garment, and adds that the Baptist evidently saw all of it, since he mentions it later. Gill insists on a detail others let pass, that it was Christ and not John who came up out of the water, having descended into the river and been baptized by immersion, and that he came up out of the river itself and not merely from the water's edge; and for the voice he supplies the Jewish name, the Bath Kol. Henry hears in the whole scene the end of a long obscurity, and asks how much hidden worth is lost in the dust of contempt or wrapped in the veil of humility, until, as here, it is owned.

Why a sinless man should be baptized at all is answered four ways that do not quite agree. Pseudo-Chrysostom argues from the nature of the rite: John's baptism was incomplete beside Christ's and different from the Jewish, standing between both, and by submitting to it he showed that he was not baptized for remission nor as wanting the Holy Ghost, but to be made known to all and to fulfil all righteousness, so that earthly things might be joined to heavenly. Bede makes it an approval of John's baptism and a sanctifying of the waters, so that the descent of the dove might show the coming of the Holy Ghost in the laver of believers. Henry reads it as humility owning God, Christ taking the likeness of sinful flesh and being washed as if he had been polluted, though perfectly unspotted. Pseudo-Chrysostom adds the guard the others leave implicit, that the Spirit is not said to have descended as though then first coming to him, for he had never left him, but to show forth the Christ and point him out as by the finger of faith.
10:
The opened heaven and the dove are read for what they signify rather than what they were. Bede denies any unclosing of the elements and puts the opening in the eyes of the spirit, or else says it was done for our sakes, to whom the door of the kingdom is opened by the laver of regeneration; the dove suits because it is an animal of great simplicity, far removed from the malice of gall, and it sat on the head of Jesus lest anyone think the voice was addressed to John. On abiding he is exact: this is peculiar to Christ, that the Spirit once filling him should never leave him, whereas the grace given to disciples for signs and miracles is sometimes taken away. Henry marks a difference between the two reports, that Matthew has the heavens opened to him while Mark has him see them opened, and observes that many have heaven opened to receive them and do not see it. Pseudo-Jerome opens instead with a figure for the evangelist himself, a hart longing after the fountains of water and a bee that sips the tops of the flowers, and runs the dove of the Canticles through its titles, bride in the Patriarchs and beloved in John the Baptist.

The wording of the voice is a reported difference that one witness declines to settle. Robertson notes that Mark and Luke have Thou art where Matthew has This is, and in thee where Matthew has in whom. Augustine states the reason for Matthew's form, that the bystanders might know which of them was the Son of God, and then refuses to choose: take which you will, only remember that the Evangelists relate the same meaning though not the same form of speaking. Bede adds that the words did not inform the Son of anything he did not know but show us what we ought to believe, and finds the mystery of the Trinity set out in the scene, the Son baptized, the Spirit descending, the Father bearing witness. Robertson records the misuse the verse has been put to, the Cerinthian Gnostics taking the dove for a heavenly Christ who came upon the man Jesus and left him at the Cross, which he calls a forecast of the modern distinction between the Jesus of history and the theological Christ. Henry preserves the stranger traditions without endorsing them, that Justin Martyr says a fire was kindled in Jordan and that an ancient report has a great light shining round the place.
12:
The verb that sends him out is the chapter's most contested word. Robertson calls it vivid and bolder than the other Gospels, and notes that it is the same word Mark uses for driving out demons. Clarke renders it putteth him forth against Matthew's was brought up. Barnes will not let the force stand unqualified, insisting that it does not mean he was compelled forcibly against his will, but that he was inclined or led there by the Spirit for important purposes. Chrysostom takes the harshness as deliberate and doctrinal: the text does not simply say he went, so that we may understand the going was according to the word of Divine Providence, and so that we may learn that no man should thrust himself into temptation while those who are as it were driven into it remain conquerors. Bede guards the same word from the opposite misreading, observing that Luke has purposely premised that Jesus was full of the Spirit when he returned from Jordan, lest the evil spirit be thought to have had any power over him. Ellicott simply flags the characteristic adverb and the stronger verb as Mark's own, and Robertson adds that the forty days in the wilderness were under the direct guidance of the Holy Spirit. Chrysostom presses the motive a step further, that the Spirit drove him because he designed to provoke the devil to tempt him, giving him an opportunity not only by hunger but also by the place.

What the forty days are for divides into discipline and arithmetic. Chrysostom makes the whole episode instruction: it happened after the baptism so that every baptized person might sustain greater temptations afterwards without being troubled, since the devil approaches only where he has seen a man set in a place of greater honour, and thrusts himself in most when he sees men remaining solitary. Bede reads the number as a figure of the whole time of this world, the globe being divided into four quarters and the Commandments being ten, so that four times ten is forty; and he reads day and night as prosperity and adversity, in both of which the adversary is at hand. Wesley states the rule more shortly, that in all the children of God extraordinary manifestations of favour are wont to be followed by extraordinary temptations. Henry adds the practical observation that retirement from the world is an opportunity of freer converse with God, and must sometimes be chosen even by those called to the greatest business.
13:
The wild beasts are peculiar to Mark, and every witness makes something different of them. Clarke calls the circumstance curious, mentioned by none of the other evangelists, and takes it to place him in the most remote and savage part of the desert, perhaps as an emblem of the brutal cruelty with which he was afterwards persecuted. Ellicott lists what the creatures might have been, the panther, the bear, the wolf, the hyena and possibly the lion, and reads their presence as adding to the terrors while his preservation fulfilled the promise in the very Psalm from which the Tempter drew his chief weapon. Robertson supplies the same bestiary for the night and borrows from Swete the observation that the promise of victory over the beasts stands immediately after the promise of angelic guardianship that Satan had quoted. Lightfoot reads the untouched safety backwards, to Adam before his fall. Henry takes it as his Father's care, and an earnest that the same care would feed him when hungry, since special protections are earnests of seasonable supplies; he also hears an intimation of the generation he was to live among, no better than wild beasts, nay abundantly worse.

When the angels came is a smaller disagreement, and the figurative readings close the scene. Barnes places the ministry after the days of temptation had expired, reasoning from the other Gospels that he ate nothing during them. Lightfoot divides the two by their visibility instead, forty days of invisible temptation with angels ministering visibly throughout, and has Satan at the last put on the appearance of an angel of light, pretending to wait on him as the rest did and hiding his hook the more artificially. Wesley agrees that the visible temptation followed, and remarks that Mark gives not only a compendium of Matthew but several valuable particulars the others omitted. Pseudo-Chrysostom draws the general rule, that to those who conquer in temptation angels stand near and minister. Pseudo-Jerome reads the peace with the beasts as the peace of the ark, where clean animals lodged with unclean, and finds it wherever the flesh does not lust against the spirit. Bede divides the two natures between the two halves of the verse: Christ dwells among the wild beasts as man, and as God uses the ministry of Angels.
14:
The chapter jumps a year, and two witnesses say so plainly. Bede warns that no one should suppose the imprisonment followed immediately on the forty days, since whoever reads the Gospel of John will find that the Lord taught many things and did many miracles before it, and reports the tradition that John, having read the other three and approved their text as true, saw that they had composed the history of only the year after the Baptist was cast into prison, and so related the earlier period they had passed over. Robertson says the same thing in modern terms: but for the Fourth Gospel we should not know of the year of work in Perea, Galilee, Judea and Samaria preceding the Galilean ministry, and it was the arrest of John that had much to do with the departure from Judea. Ellicott simply notes that Mark agrees with Matthew in omitting the early ministry and takes the imprisonment as his starting-point, assuming it known though not narrating it until much later; Gill supplies the missing facts, the castle where Herod held him and the reproof that put him there.

Why Jesus withdrew rather than stayed is read as prudence by some and as doctrine by others. Barnes makes it deliberate caution — he supposed that if he remained in Judea Herod would attempt his life also, his time of death had not come, and we may learn from it that when we have great duties to perform we are not wantonly to endanger our lives, and are to secure them whenever it can be done without a sacrifice of principle. Pseudo-Chrysostom takes the same act as instruction, that he goes back into Galilee teaching us not to resist the violence of evil men, and that he retired to keep himself for teaching and healing before he suffered. Theophylact draws the rule out in full: in persecutions we ought to retire and not await them, but when we fall into them we must sustain them. Henry turns the sequence into a promise, that the silencing of Christ's ministers shall not be the suppressing of Christ's gospel, since if some be laid aside others shall be raised up, perhaps mightier than they.
15:
What the fulfilled time means is answered from prophecy and from grammar. Clarke and Wesley both point to the term specified by Daniel, Clarke adding that nothing is done but according to a plan laid by the Divine wisdom and never performed till the appointed time was filled up. Gill offers two references and does not choose between them, either the end of the legal dispensation and the Jewish church state, or the fulness of time for the Messiah's appearance agreed between the Father and the Son. Ellicott notes that the clause is absent from the parallel passages and carries the same thought as the fulness of time in the Apostle. Robertson works on the word itself, which is the term for an opportunity or crisis rather than time in general, and observes that Mark also adds the call to believe to the bare command to repent. On the name of the kingdom, Origen holds that the kingdom of God and the kingdom of heaven are essentially the same though they differ in idea, and that the kingdom of God is confined neither by place nor by time; Theophylact makes it a conversation according to the Gospel, so that a man in the flesh living by it may be said to have the kingdom of heaven.

Whether repentance and faith are one demand or two is the entry's real dispute. Calvin puts the question directly — since repentance depends on the Gospel, why does Mark separate it from believing? — and gives two answers: that God sometimes calls us to repentance meaning only that we should change our life, and afterwards shows that newness of life is his own gift, so that duty is enjoined and the grace of obedience offered at once; and that the faith here enjoined relates chiefly to the forgiveness of sins. Henry insists that the two must be held together, that reforming our lives will not save us without trusting the righteousness of Christ, nor trusting Christ without reformation of heart and life, and that what Christ has joined no man should put asunder. Bede reaches the same balance from the other side: renounce dead works, for of what use is believing without good works, and yet the merit of good works does not bring a man to faith, but faith begins in order that good works may follow. Pseudo-Jerome argues it by images instead, that he who would have the kernel breaks the shell, that the sweetness of the apple makes up for the bitterness of its root, and that the hope of gain makes the dangers of the sea pleasant.
16:
The call by the sea is Mark's first scene of action, and the observers notice how it is staged. The Gloss marks the transition, that having given the preaching to the multitude the Evangelist turns to the disciples whom he made ministers of that preaching. Robertson catches the camerawork, Mark using the word for alongside twice over to make the picture realistic, and reads the participle as casting on both sides, now on one hand and now on the other, a haul rather than a single throw; he notes further that the four were partners in a trade, that the detail of going a little further is Mark's own, and that mending the nets means getting ready to succeed better at the next cast. Clarke contributes the one textual point, that the best manuscripts and versions read the brother of Simon rather than his brother, and that the most eminent critics approve it. Ellicott notices that Mark names Simon here without adding Peter. Theophylact reads the summons as leaving no interval at all, that we must not allow any time to lapse but follow the Lord at once, and Robertson observes that the trade word describes fishing with a net, a cast made for a haul rather than a single throw.

Whether this was their first meeting with Jesus is disputed, and both answers come with evidence. Theophylact makes it plainly a second calling: Peter and Andrew had been disciples of the Forerunner and joined Jesus when John bore witness, then, grieving that John had been cast into prison, went back to their trade, which is where this scene finds them. Bede faces the harder problem, that Luke tells the story differently, with James and John called to help the others and the saying about catching men addressed to Peter alone, and the men following only after they had brought their ships to land; he resolves it in sequence, that Luke's transaction happened first and they afterwards returned to their fishing as their custom was, so that what Mark relates came later — and the proof is in the boats, which are not drawn ashore here, as they would have been by men meaning to return. Gill reaches the same result by a different road, that Jesus was looking out for them, having appointed them to this service long before.
18:
The trade they left is made to mean several things at once. Bede takes the choice as evidential, that fishers and unlettered men are sent to preach so that the faith of believers might be thought to lie in the power of God and not in eloquence or learning. Theophylact adds a moral qualification, that they lived on their own labours and not on the fruits of iniquity, and that such men were worthy to be the first disciples. Remigius turns the trade into its own figure and then inverts it: by the net of preaching they drew men from the depths of infidelity to the light of faith, and the fishing is wonderful because fishes when caught soon die while men caught by the word are rather made alive. Robertson keeps to the verb Mark alone supplies, that they would become fishers of men, which he reads as a slow and long process that Jesus undertook and would finish, preachers being made out of laymen willing to leave their business.

The family left behind draws the sharpest comment. Theophylact reads the departure as exemplary and pushes it into a precept, that they left their father because he would have hindered them, and that the reader hindered by parents should do likewise; he infers from the silence that Zebedee was not a believer, while the mother of the Apostles was, since she followed Christ after Zebedee was dead. Ellicott and Robertson read the same verse for its social detail instead, the hired servants being peculiar to this Gospel and throwing light on the relative position of the family, since Zebedee and his sons evidently had an extensive business in co-operation with the others, which would go on without them. Robertson turns it into a modern question, whether a young man can leave father and mother to become a fisher of men, and notes that the sacrifice falls on the home folks who carry the additional burden. Wesley marks only the speed of it, that from this time they forsook their employ and constantly attended him, and calls them happy who follow Christ at the first call. Pseudo-Jerome ends where allegory must, with the four drawing us to heaven like the chariot of Elias, and their names read as obedience, manliness, supplanting and grace.
21:
The scene changes to a synagogue on a sabbath, and the first remarks are about how the book is put together. Pseudo-Jerome says outright that Mark arranges the sayings as they stood in his own mind rather than in themselves, quitting the order of the history and following the order of the mysteries, which is why the first miracle falls on a sabbath. Ellicott marks the seam differently, that from here the narrative ceases to run parallel with Matthew and agrees almost verbally with Luke, and takes the occasion to count the adverb the English version disguises as immediately or anon, which occurs forty-one times in the Gospel and nine times in this chapter alone. Robertson fills in the setting: the tense means he began to teach as soon as he entered; Capernaum had become his headquarters after the rejection at Nazareth; the ruins of the synagogue have been found with the stones in good preservation and there is even talk of restoring the building. Gill notes that the verb is plural, so that the four newly called disciples went in with him, though some versions and a copy known to Beza read the singular.

How a layman came to be preaching at all is answered from custom. Barnes explains that the presiding elder, after the reading of the Scriptures, invited any who chose to address the people, and that although the Saviour was neither a priest of the Levitical order nor an officer of the synagogue he often availed himself of the privilege. Robertson describes the same service as prayer, praise, reading and exposition by any rabbi or other competent person, and recalls the attendant whose business it was to bring out the precious manuscript and return it to its place. Theophylact supplies the reason behind the institution, that the Law commanded rest on that day precisely so that they might meet together to attend to sacred reading.

What the astonishment was at is the entry's real question, and the answers divide between matter and manner. Ellicott holds that the stress falls on the manner rather than the thing taught, and notes that the verbal agreement with the parallel suggests Mark had heard or read it. Gill will not separate them, finding the people struck both by a doctrine they had not been used to hear and by a manner full of gracefulness, gravity and majesty. Calvin puts it entirely in the preaching: the power of the Spirit shone there with such brightness as to extort admiration even from irreligious and cold hearers, whereas the Scribes were false expounders whose doctrine was literal and dead and destitute of majesty — a coldness he says may be observed still in the speculative theology of Popery, where the masters thunder magisterially and their controversies exhibit no traces of religion. Clarke locates it in the commission instead, since the Scribes had no authority from God, the matter of their teaching not coming from him and the teachers not being sent by him. Bede specifies the difference exactly: the Scribes taught what was written in Moses and the Prophets, while Jesus, as the God and Lord of Moses, by the freedom of his own will either added what appeared wanting in the Law or altered it, in the manner of it was said to them of old time, but I say unto you. Robertson agrees and sharpens the contrast, that the Scribes quoted other rabbis and made the traditions a millstone about the necks of the people, so that the crowd saw at once a personality whose authority came direct from God.
24:
The name the spirit uses is examined from both ends. Henry thinks the title Jesus of Nazareth was chosen to fix low thoughts in the people, since no good thing was expected out of Nazareth and the Messiah must come from Bethlehem. Pseudo-Chrysostom works on the second title: the word for spirit is used of an Angel, of the air, of the soul and of the Holy Ghost, so the evangelist adds unclean to prevent confusion; and the confession calls him holy not as one of many, for every prophet was holy, but by the article shows him to be the One. Ellicott traces the phrase to its source, noting that it occurs only here, in the parallel, and in the better manuscripts of the Fourth Gospel, and probably originated in a Messianic reading of an older text. Barnes explains the title by three things, that he was eminently pure, that he was the only begotten Son equal with the Father, and that he was anointed to the work of Mediator. Robertson notes a textual detail with a theological edge, that the better reading is the singular I know though some manuscripts give the plural, the man speaking for the demon and for himself at once.

Whether the confession was welcome is where the witnesses part. Calvin reads it as a trick: the devil dexterously acknowledges Christ in order to insinuate into men's minds a suspicion that there was some secret understanding between them, which is the reason Christ rebukes him, and while flattering him he indirectly withdraws himself from his power, wishing Christ would be satisfied with an empty title and exercise it on nobody. Pseudo-Chrysostom generalises the refusal into a precept, that the Truth did not wish the witness of unclean spirits and that we should not believe devils however they may proclaim the truth. Theophylact takes it the other way and finds the confession useful, so that the bystanders might know from how great an evil the man was freed and might believe on account of the miracle. Augustine explains what such knowledge is worth: there was in them knowledge but not charity, since they feared their punishment and did not love the righteousness, and he was known to them not as eternal Life, as the holy Angels enjoy him, but by some temporal effects of his power and in terror. Henry says the same in a sentence, that those who have only a notion that he is the holy One of God go no further than the devil does.

The plural in let us alone is read three ways. Barnes takes the one spirit to speak in the name of others leagued together in the work of evil, each knowing that the punishment of one would be shared; and he answers the question behind it, that what have we to do with thee amounts to a claim that no injury was done, which was untrue, the possession being a direct assault on God and his works. Clarke settles the idiom philologically, showing the same construction in the Hebrew of an older quarrel and in its Greek rendering, and concludes that the demoniac spoke in Hebrew or in the dialect then common in Judea. Lightfoot opens a third possibility, that the us may be the Galileans in the synagogue rather than the devils, since the masters taught that in the generation when the Son of David came Galilee should be laid waste and the Galileans wander from city to city; if that report was current, the spirit had a fit occasion for frightening them out of receiving Christ. Bede, meanwhile, reconciles the tearing with the other account of a man not hurt, taking the vexing to be the casting into the midst, so that the tossing of his limbs did not weaken him — devils being wont to come out even with the cutting away of limbs.
23:
Mark's phrase is that the man was in an unclean spirit, and both the moderns and Henry stop on it. Henry reads it as possession rather than affliction, the spirit having the man and leading him captive, as a man is said to be in a fever or in a frenzy; and he reports the opinion that it is more proper to say the body is in the soul, because governed by it, than the soul in the body. Robertson identifies the idiom as the one behind in Christ and in the Lord, so that the spirit was in the man and the man in the spirit, and notes that Jesus nevertheless distinguishes between the two. On why the man was in the synagogue at all, Clarke and Barnes agree that he must have had lucid intervals, since otherwise he would not have been admitted, and Barnes supposes a fit came on while he was there; Ellicott answers from custom instead, that in most Eastern cities madness had an immunity from restraint, and the demoniacs seem to have mingled at will with the worshippers. Henry alone suspects design, that the man came neither to be taught nor healed but, as some think, to confront Christ and hinder people from believing.

What the phrase unclean adds is asked by the fathers and answered two ways. Pseudo-Chrysostom takes it as a precaution against ambiguity, since the word for spirit is used of an Angel, of the air, of the soul and of the Holy Ghost, and the adjective fixes which is meant; and he grounds the name in the thing, the spirit being called unclean for his impiousness, his far removal from God, and his employment in all unclean and wicked works. Clarke narrows it to a particular vice, suggesting that this spirit filled the heart of the man he possessed with lascivious thoughts and desires, and warns that by giving way to the first attacks of such a spirit a man may soon let him take full possession of the whole soul. Theophylact turns from the man to the tenant and finds him miserable on his own terms: to come out of a man the devil counts his own perdition, for devils are ruthless and think they suffer some evil so long as they are not troubling men.

That the first miracle should be an exorcism is treated as fitting rather than accidental. Bede gives the reason in a sentence: since by the envy of the devil death first entered into the world, it was right that the medicine of healing should first work against the author of death; and he adds that the devils, seeing the Lord on the earth, thought they were immediately to be judged. Pseudo-Jerome finds the fitness in the place and the day instead, reading Capernaum as the town of consolation and the sabbath as rest, so that the man with an evil spirit is healed by rest and consolation and the setting agrees with the cure; and he enlarges the single man into the human race, in which uncleanness reigned from Adam to Moses. Robertson, who elsewhere calls the whole subject of demonology difficult though no more so than the problem of the devil, keeps the question open and wonders aloud whether the confirmed criminals of his own day are not under a like power, the only cure being conversion.
25:
The rebuke is aimed past the man, and the witnesses are careful about that. Barnes observes that Jesus did not once address the man but spoke to the spirit, and draws the conclusion he wants from it: this proves the case was not mere disease or derangement, for how could the Son of God hold converse with disease or delirium, whereas here was a being that conversed, reasoned, cavilled, felt, resisted and knew him. Gill reads the command as a refusal of a testimony that was not wanted, lest it should be thought there was a confederacy between them. Wesley states the principle in full, that Christ would suffer those evil spirits to speak neither in opposition to him nor in favour of him, since he needed not their testimony and would not encourage it, lest any should infer that he acted in concert with them. Clarke draws a pastoral moral instead, that a spirit of this cast will yield only to the sovereign power of the Son of God, and that all watchings, fastings and mortifications considered in themselves will do little or no good.

The word rendered hold thy peace is stronger than the English, and everyone says so differently. Ellicott gives it as be still or be gagged, and notes that the same verb is used when the winds and the waves are calmed. Robertson insists on the animal image, that it means be muzzled, as an ox is muzzled in the law about treading out the corn, and canvasses the renderings of others, one translator's be quiet as too mild, another's shut up as nearer, though shut your mouth would be too colloquial, and a third's gagged as belonging properly to a different verb. Barnes lets the force stand as it is and calls the silencing a signal proof of power, that a word could quiet an evil angel and compel him against his will to leave a man he delighted to torment.

How violent the departure was is the one place where the accounts have to be squared. Gill states the problem and the answer together: no limb was torn away and no wound made, since the other Gospel says he hurt him not, but he shook him, threw him into the midst and laid him prostrate in convulsions. Ellicott simply records the added clause. Calvin agrees that the two writers mean the same thing and that the design of both was to show the devil going out in a violent manner, the man thrown down as if he were to be torn; but he will not make the escape quite clean, allowing that the attack was not in no degree whatever attended by injury or at least by some feeling of pain, only that the man was afterwards delivered and restored to perfect health. Robertson describes the motion clinically, a convulsing like a spasm, the word used by medical writers of the turning of the stomach, and adds the screech that Mark alone records.

The last struggle is read as a portrait of malice. Barnes makes it general: still malignant though doomed to obey, submitting because obliged and not because he chose, the spirit exerted his last power and inflicted all the pain he could before bowing and coming out, which is the nature of an evil disposition, making even the appearance of obedience an occasion for further mischief. Clarke turns the same observation into counsel for the tempted, that never was a person possessed who did not suffer a convulsion, and that when the propensities of the flesh are most violent in someone determined to serve God it is often a proof that these are the last efforts of the impure spirit, who rages because he knows his time is short.
27:
The crowd's reaction is reported as a jumble, and Robertson thinks that is exactly the point. They questioned among themselves by look and word, he says, and the position of the phrase about authority is equivocal — it may belong to the new teaching or to the commanding — which he attributes, with Swete, to Mark giving the incoherent and excited remarks of the crowd in their natural form. Ellicott notes that a variant reading yields a different structure altogether, and insists that the word rendered doctrine means the teaching taken as a whole, manner as well as substance. Clarke reports that there is a vast diversity in the manuscripts on this verse, and says he has added a conjunction from the Syriac to separate the members of the sentence.

What exactly was new divides into the teaching and the power behind it. Barnes says the novelty was the casting out: it was done by a word, in his own name and by his own authority, which proved him superior to all the unclean spirits, and from it the impression became prevalent that he was the Messiah. Clarke puts the two together and lets the crowd draw the inference — they had never heard such a gracious doctrine nor seen teaching supported by miracles, and other men are brought into subjection by unclean spirits while this person subjects unclean spirits to himself. Robertson dwells on the freshness of the teaching itself, original as the dew of the morning on blossoms just blown, and a novelty in a synagogue where only staid and stilted rabbinical rules had heretofore been droned out; but he thinks the most astonishing thing of all is the obedience, since the people were used to the magical formulae of Jewish exorcists and this was utterly different. Calvin defends the crowd's word against any charge of disparagement, holding that they call it doctrine not by way of reproach but as an acknowledgment of something unusual and extraordinary, and locates their only fault in remaining at hesitation, whereas the children of God ought to make increasing progress. Bede connects the two halves of the day, that seeing the power of the miracle they wonder at the newness of the doctrine and are roused to search into what they had heard by what they had seen.

The spreading of the report is where an old habit of Mark's is finally weighed. The Gloss supplies the mechanism in a line, that what men wonder at they soon divulge, out of the abundance of the heart. Clarke lists three reasons the news travelled — the miracle was great, it evidenced much benevolence in the worker of it, and it was very public, being wrought in the synagogue — and then turns on the adverb that carried it, observing that the word rendered immediately occurs more frequently in this evangelist than in any other writer of the new covenant, that it is very often superfluous, and that it may often be omitted in translation without prejudice to the sense, being used much as the older English writers used forsooth. Ellicott had already counted the same word and drawn the opposite conclusion, that its frequent recurrence should be noticed as the reader proceeds. Robertson closes on the simple fact of it, that with no telephones, telegraphs, newspapers or radio, news had a marvellous way of spreading by word of mouth throughout all Galilee.
29:
The move from synagogue to house is small, and the witnesses use it for chronology and for character. Calvin takes it as evidence that Matthew did not observe the order of time, since Mark expressly says only four disciples were with him and has him go straight from the synagogue to the house. Robertson fills in the household: Peter was married before he began to follow Jesus and lived there with his brother, his wife and her mother, and Mark heard the story from Peter himself, told of his own house, where Jesus made his home while in Capernaum. Henry draws the manners out of it, that Christ did not sit still when his name was up, as some think they may lie in bed once their reputation is made, and that coming from a synagogue where he had taught with divine authority he conversed familiarly with poor fishermen and did not think it below him, accepting such entertainment as a fisherman could give. Theophylact supplies the ordinary reason for the visit, that he retired about evening, as the custom was on that day, to eat in his disciples' house.

How ill she was, and how the cure came, is where the accounts are compared. Gill calls it a great fever, violent enough to threaten death and dangerous in an old person, and is careful about the gesture: he took her hand not to feel her pulse and judge the disorder as physicians do, nor merely in the customary friendly way, but in order to restore her. Robertson sets the three descriptions side by side — Mark has her lying prostrate and burning, Matthew has her stretched out, Luke uses a technical medical phrase — and notes that all three report the recovery and the ministering with no convalescence between, Mark and Matthew giving the touch on the hand and Luke showing Jesus standing over her like a doctor. Calvin thinks the touch deliberate, since he might have done it by the slightest expression of his will, and ascribes it either to affection or to the usefulness of an outward sign at that time. Whether he was asked is itself disputed: Bede notes that the other account has them beseech him for her, and concludes that the Saviour heals sometimes after being asked and sometimes of his own accord; Pseudo-Chrysostom has the disciples not waiting for the evening but praying at once.

The recovery is read for what it is for. Henry marks that the fever, leaving her, did not leave her weak as fevers do, and that the hand which healed her strengthened her, the cure being ordered to action, to fit us to minister to Christ and to those who are his. Bede says the same and makes the completeness the point: the health conferred at the Lord's command returns at once entire, with such strength that she can serve those whose help she had needed. He also takes the day as doctrine, that in giving his gifts of healing so profusely on a sabbath Christ teaches that he is not under the Law but above it, and does not choose the Jewish sabbath but the true one. The allegorists then read the fever. Bede pairs the two cures morally, the man delivered from the devil standing for the soul purged of unclean thoughts and the woman cured of a fever for the flesh restrained from the heat of concupiscence. Theophylact makes the fever anger, since a man in the unruliness of his anger stretches out his hands to do hurt, and if reason restrains them he will arise and serve reason; and he reads her ministering as a promise, that God will heal a sick man who ministers to the Saints through love of Christ. Pseudo-Jerome takes the fever for intemperance, cured by the hand of discipline and the lifting up of our desires.
32:
The crowd waits for sunset, and everyone explains why. Gill and Wesley give the reckoning, that the Jews counted the sabbath from sunset to sunset, so that when the last of the two evening days had come and the sun was down the restraint was over. Theophylact makes the motive explicit, that the multitude thought it not lawful to heal on that day and therefore waited. Henry allows the scruple without approving it, observing that Christ had proved it lawful to heal on a sabbath but that if any stumbled at it they were welcome at another time, and that their weakness was no prejudice to them in applying to him. Robertson watches the mechanics: the tense shows a steady stream, and the other account adds that Jesus laid his hand on every one of them as they passed by in grateful procession. Ellicott names the two features peculiar to Mark here, the fuller description of the whole city gathered at the door and the omission of Matthew's reference to the prophecy.

The gathering at the door is Mark's own detail, and it draws the warmest writing in the chapter. Robertson thinks the evangelist is seeing with Peter's eyes again, and imagines Peter watching with pride and gratitude as Jesus stood in the doorway healing the crowds in the glory of that sunset, a scene he loved to tell afterwards. Henry sees the same crowd less fondly, gathered at the door as beggars for a dole, and turns it into an argument, that others speeding well with Christ should quicken our own enquiries after him. Wesley looks past the scene to what became of it and asks what a fair prospect was here, and who could then have imagined that all these blossoms would die away without fruit. Henry takes the crowded doorway as a pattern for the hours after public worship, since Christ was flocked after in a private house as well as in the synagogue, and calls his word a salve for every sore. Robertson notes that the phrase for the diseases means many-coloured or variegated, so that all sorts of sick folk came and were healed, and Barnes reduces the whole city to a great part of it. Pseudo-Jerome reads the door itself, making the door of the kingdom repentance and faith, which works health for various diseases, since divers are the vices with which the city of this world is sick.
34:
The word many is read two contradictory ways, and both readings are in the chapter. Theophylact takes it strictly and makes it a limit: he says many because there were faithless persons who could not be cured at all on account of their unfaithfulness, so that he healed many of those brought, that is, all who had faith. Pseudo-Chrysostom takes it loosely and makes it a total, holding that in the Scripture mode of expression many is to be understood as all, and explains the difference from the other Gospel by Mark's habit of passing over things for brevity. Bede leaves the number alone and reads the hour instead, taking the setting of the sun for the passion of him who said he was the light of the world while he was in it, and finding it significant that more were healed as the sun went down, since he who taught a few Jews in the flesh has transmitted faith and health to all the Gentiles.

Why the demons were silenced is answered four ways that do not conflict so much as accumulate. Barnes and Calvin both give the reason of timing, that the hour had not come when Christ wished his name promulgated; Calvin adds the stronger reason and prefers it, that he refused to have as heralds and witnesses of his divinity those whose praise could only soil and injure his character, since the prince of death is in irreconcilable enmity with the Author of eternal life. Pseudo-Augustine makes it a lesson for the reader, that we are not to believe devils even when they say true, because once they find people who believe them they mingle truth with falsehood; and he distinguishes what they knew, that they saw in him all the signs foretold by the Prophets and recognised the Christ, while remaining ignorant of his divinity. Bede presses that distinction into an explanation of the crucifixion: the devil, having failed by tempting to prove whether he was the Son of God, now suspected it from the miracles, and urged the Jews on not because he doubted but because he did not foresee that he himself would be condemned by that death. Robertson notes only that testimony from such a source was not calculated to help the cause, and Clarke reports that the clause naming the Christ is added by several ancient and respectable manuscripts but appears to be only a gloss. Wesley uses the verse to demolish a theory, that if the possessed were merely diseased persons, as one physician had argued, then Christ suffered not the diseases to say that they knew him.
35:
The hour is stated so precisely that it must be reconciled with the other account, and the moderns do the arithmetic. Barnes points out that Luke says it was day, and argues that Mark does not mean literally a great while before day but very early, while there was yet much appearance of night, so that both describe the same moment at daybreak. Robertson fixes it in the last watch of the night, between three and six, with the phrase meaning the early part of that watch while it was still a little dark, and reads the tense as picturing him praying through the early hours. Clarke gives the word the whole space of three hours that finished the fourth watch. Ellicott notes that the note of time is peculiar to Mark, and that prayer seems to have been sought here, as at other times, after a day of extraordinary and exhausting labour. Gill adds that this was the morrow after the sabbath, and that he rose in spite of the fatigue of the day before.

Why a sinless man prayed at all, and why in secret, draws answers of two kinds. Clarke denies any need in him, since in him dwelt all the fullness of the Godhead bodily, and takes the prayer for a pattern, holding that everything our Lord did he performed either as our pattern or as our sacrifice. Pseudo-Chrysostom says the same, that it was not that he required prayer, for it was he who received the prayers of men, but that he did it by way of an economy and became to us the model of good work. Theophylact draws the lesson from the solitude, that we are not to do anything for the sake of appearance nor to publish our good openly, and that we ought to attribute to God whatever we do well. Barnes turns the verse into a rule of life: the Saviour sought a place far from the world and even from his disciples, he did it first upon rising, and the religious enjoyment of a whole day will be according to the state of the heart in the morning — a reproach to those who spend the precious hours of the morning in sleep. Bede reads the dawn typologically: if the setting sun meant the death of the Saviour, the returning dawn may mean his resurrection.

The retreat is also read as a retreat from something, and here the witnesses differ. Robertson collects the modern guesses without settling them — one calls it a flight from the unexpected reality into which his conception of his calling had brought him; another holds that he withdrew before his sudden popularity, to pray that he might not be ensnared by it or induced to accept the ways of ease instead of duty; a third has him leaving in the night with a preaching tour already planned and opposition feared — and remarks that many a preacher can understand the mood. The pursuit is described in strong words. Robertson notes that the verb belongs to the hunt or the chase, so that Peter and the others hunted him out, and quotes the judgement that Simon's intention was good, since the Master seemed to be losing precious opportunities and had to be brought back. Clarke reads it more warmly, that they followed him eagerly, having begun to taste the good word of God and thinking they could never hear too much, and regrets how often that spirit is lost after conversion. Ellicott observes that Mark alone names who followed while Luke alone gives the motive, that they would have kept him at Capernaum. Barnes says plainly that the report was meant to draw him out of his retirement, and Clarke sorts the seekers by motive: some to hear, some to be healed, some to be saved, and some through no good motive.
38:
The word Mark uses for where they are going is rare enough to need explaining, and three witnesses explain it. Ellicott says the compound occurs here only, that it means village cities, and that it seems to have been coined for places like Bethsaida and Chorazin on the lake shore, more than villages yet hardly to be classed as cities. Gill defines it the same way, towns that were neither villages nor cities but between both, and notes that several versions simply render it villages and cities; he adds that the places meant are those which had synagogues. Lightfoot goes behind the Greek to the rabbinic distinction and quotes the rule that a man cannot compel his wife to move from town to city nor from city to town, with the reason given plainly, that in a city anything is to be had and in a town it is not, a city being a place of broad streets where the neighbouring inhabitants meet at a market. Clarke records the variant, that the Codex Bezae, most versions and all the Itala read neighbouring villages and cities. Robertson finds the decision itself surprising, that Jesus should leave the eager excited throngs of Capernaum for country towns without walls or much importance.

Whether an itinerant ministry is the better kind is raised here as a genuine question. Calvin asks it directly — is it better that the ministers of the Gospel should run here and there, giving only a slight and partial taste in each place, or that they should remain and instruct perfectly the hearers they have once obtained? — and answers for the particular case rather than in general, that the design was agreeable to the call of the Father and founded on the best reasons, since Christ had to travel throughout Judea within a short period to awaken men on all sides as if by the sound of a trumpet. Clarke turns the same verse into a standing rule and will not qualify it: the towns and the villages will not come to the preacher, the preacher must go to them, and no minister should think he has delivered his own soul till he has made an offer of salvation to every city and village within his reach. Barnes reads the logic of the sentence as a refusal of concentration, that since multitudes press to hear he will not remain, having been sent not to preach at Capernaum only. Theophylact gives the same thought a figure, that it was not right to shut up doctrine in one place but to throw out his rays everywhere, and that he passes on to those more in need.
39:
The clause about coming forth is the one place where the witnesses reach past the itinerary. Ellicott allows that in this form the words might refer simply to leaving Capernaum, and only the other Gospel's was I sent connects them with the mission as a whole; he adds the honest qualification that the disciples at this stage would hardly have entered into the full meaning, and would have understood a coming forth from his home at Nazareth rather than from the bosom of the Father. Barnes takes the larger sense without hesitation, that he came forth from God. Pseudo-Chrysostom makes the two reports complementary rather than rival, finding in Mark's wording the mystery of his emptying himself and the sovereignty of his divine nature, since he asserts that he came willingly into the world, while the other form proclaims the Dispensation and the good pleasure of the Father. He also explains the dismissal of the crowd charitably, that Christ received them willingly and chose to send them away so that the rest might be partakers, since he was not to remain long in the world.

On the tour itself the record is thin, and two witnesses say so in their own ways. Robertson calls it the first tour of Galilee and observes flatly that we are told little about this great preaching tour. Augustine fills part of the gap by identifying what belongs inside it, holding that the sermon delivered on the mount, which Matthew gives and Mark has entirely passed over, falls within this preaching, Mark having repeated only some of its sentences in scattered places and out of continuous order. Clarke reads the tense as continuance — he kept preaching, never slackened his pace, since immortal souls were perishing for lack of knowledge — and makes the diligence a charge upon the ministry of his own day. Theophylact notices that the teaching and the casting out of devils are reported together, and draws the practical conclusion that unless Christ had shown forth miracles his teaching would not have been believed, so that the reader too should work after teaching lest his word be fruitless.
40:
The leper's approach is read for its posture and its theology together. Robertson notes that the kneeling is a picturesque detail some manuscripts omit, and that Luke has him fall on his face. Bede takes the gesture as at once lowliness and shame, meant to show that every man should blush for the stains of his life, and observes that the shame did not stifle the confession: he showed his wound and begged for medicine. Henry sorts the approach into three things a petitioner should bring — humility, a firm belief of the power, and submission to the will — and makes the second the practical point, that what we believe of the power of Christ we must bring home to our own case and say, thou canst do this for me. Theophylact hears the divinity implied in the phrasing, since the man did not say if thou wilt, pray unto God but if thou wilt. Clarke, who thinks Mark the best of the three to preach this from because he is the most circumstantial, lays the scene out in steps on both sides, what the leper did and what Jesus did, and makes the compassion the source of all human salvation. Augustine adds only that the circumstances Mark assembles allow one to infer this is the same man whom Matthew has cleansed after the sermon on the mount.

Whether the if was a doubt is handled carefully by those who notice it. Bede says the man doubted of the will, not as disbelieving the compassion, but as conscious of his own filth he did not presume. Henry says the same from the other side, that the reference to the will implied no doubt of Christ's readiness to help the distressed but the modesty that became a poor petitioner; and he observes that the address is not in the form of a prayer, yet Christ answered it as a request, affectionate professions of faith and resignations to him being the most prevailing petitions there are. Gill guards the compassion from misconstruction, that it was moved by the deplorable case of the man and not by any desire of popular applause. Robertson notes that the word for it belongs to Mark alone here, and Henry takes the same clause as the key to the whole cure, since it shows that Christ's power is employed by his pity, that his reasons are fetched from within himself, and that our misery is what makes us the objects of his mercy.
41:
The touch is the detail that most needs defending, and each defence is different. Chrysostom answers from the Law, which made whoever touched a leper unclean till evening: the touch shows that such uncleanness is natural and that the Law was laid down not for him but on account of mere men, and that he is himself Lord of the Law, giving health not as a servant but as the Lord. Bede gives the shorter reason, that he touched to prove he could not be defiled who frees others from pollution. Barnes reads it evidentially, that since the law counted the touch unclean, the touching was itself proof that the healing power had already gone out and that Jesus regarded the man as clean already. Henry keeps the figure: when the queen toucheth for the evil she saith, I touch, God heals, but Christ toucheth and healeth too.

How the words of the cure should be read is the one textual quarrel here, and Bede takes a side. It is not, he says, to be taken and read as many of the Latins think, I wish to cleanse thee, but Christ says I will separately and then commands be thou clean; and there is no interval between the work of God and the command, because the work is in the command. He notices too that the answer takes up the petition exactly, the man having said if thou wilt, thou canst, and the reply giving first the will and then the effect. Chrysostom makes the same observation as a confirmation of the man's faith, that Christ did not correct the opinion held of him but filled up in deed what the leper had said in word. Barnes draws the plainest inference of all, that none but God can work a miracle and that this one was worked by an exertion of his own will. Pseudo-Jerome leaves the history for the figure, making leprosy the sin of the first man which began from the head when he desired the kingdom of the world, and covetousness the root of it, as when Gehazi in an avaricious pursuit was covered with leprosy.
43:
The word for the charge is unusually strong, and the witnesses feel it differently. Robertson says it belongs to Mark alone here, that it is used of the snorting of a horse, and that it expresses powerful emotion as Jesus stood face to face with leprosy, itself a symbol of sin and all its train of evils. Gill takes the strength as directed at something specific and supposes the man was charged with the sin that had caused the disease, since leprosy was usually held to come for sin; and he sets out the rabbinic list of the things it was said to come for — a proud look, instanced from the daughters of Zion; a lying tongue, instanced from Miriam; hands that shed innocent blood, instanced from Joab, on whose head the blood of Abner and Amasa returned; and a heart that deviseth wicked imaginations. Clarke records that the verse is wanting in two copies of the Itala.

Why the silence was commanded is answered five ways, and they do not all sit together. Barnes and Wesley agree on a legal reason and state it almost identically: the priest had to pronounce the cure before the man could be readmitted, and if the story ran ahead of him, evil-minded men might prejudice the priest against declaring a healing done by Jesus to be thorough, so the official verdict is secured only by saying nothing on the way. Bede gives a doctrinal reason, that the priest might understand the leper was healed not by the Law but by a grace above the Law. Chrysostom makes it a lesson about motive, hearing in the refusal I require not thy preaching, and teaching us not to seek worldly honour as the reward of our works. Calvin gives a reason of ministry and prefers it: it was not that enemies were trying to shut his mouth but that the common people were so eager to demand miracles that no room was left for doctrine, and he wished them to be more attentive to the word than to signs. Robertson states the practical version of the same, that the prohibition was meant to allay excitement and avoid needless opposition.

What the priest was to be shown is disputed in two places. Bede anticipates the objection that the Lord seems to approve a Jewish sacrifice which the Church rejects, and answers that he had not yet offered his own holocaust in his passion, and that it was not right for significative sacrifices to be taken away before the thing they signified was confirmed. Chrysostom adds the man's own interest, that he was sent so as not to be cast out of the temple but to remain numbered with the people in prayer, and that by fulfilling every part of the Law Christ stopped the evil-speaking tongue of his critics. On the phrase about a testimony, Calvin rejects the reading that would make it a law or statute delivered to Israel, holding instead that the pronoun means the priests, so that the miracle would convict them of ingratitude if they refused Christ and take away all occasion of slander, since he had neglected not a single point of the law. Barnes reads the same words the other way, that the testimony was not to the priest but to the people, who would have the priest's own decisive verdict as evidence of a real cure.
45:
The man disobeys, and the chapter ends on the consequence. Barnes says he was so deeply affected and so rejoiced that he followed the natural dictates of his feelings rather than the command. Theophylact alone defends him outright, on the ground that the person benefited ought to be grateful and return thanks even though his benefactor requires it not. Clarke supposes he published not only his own healing but everything he had heard of the miraculous works, thinking he could never speak too much nor too well of him. Robertson turns it into an observation about human nature, that one of the best ways to spread a thing is to tell people not to tell, and adds drily that some preachers are not so disturbed by the onrush of crowds. On the clause about the city, Barnes denies that any natural inability or physical obstacle is meant, only difficulty or impropriety, probably the crowds or the risk of provoking the civil rulers; Clarke names the same fear more sharply as the jealousy of the secular government and the envy and malice of the Jewish rulers; Wesley notes that this was the very inconvenience the command to silence was meant to prevent. Clarke closes by disputing a common opinion, that of the multitudes who came from every quarter few were saved, and holds instead that thousands were brought to God by that ministry though only the constant attendants are named.

Two smaller observations round the chapter off. Ellicott notes that Mark alone makes the healed man himself the agent in spreading the report, and that his account gives in more vivid terms than the parallel both the resulting pressure of the multitude and the necessity of retiring into desert places. Robertson reads the last verb as continuous, so that even in the desert the people kept coming. Gill, who has the man going out of a synagogue, adds that the Jewish canons did allow a leper into one, provided certain rules were observed. Calvin supplies the fullest statement of what was lost by the publicity, that Christ withdrew because he saw he could not satisfy the wishes of the people without overwhelming his doctrine by a superfluity of miracles.
